summary: Describes how a restarting OSPF router can signal its neighbors that it is restarting, so they do not drop it and routing keeps working. Hello packets would otherwise cause neighbors to forget the router. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: If a friend steps out briefly, you want them to say be right back, so you keep their seat. This lets a rebooting router say that to its neighbors.

questions: how does ospf graceful restart work
what is the ospf rs bit
how does ospf avoid resetting adjacencies on restart
subtitle: A vendor-specific Hello bit that tells OSPF neighbors a router is restarting, so they keep their adjacencies.

tldr.problem: A router that restarts its OSPF software may not remember its neighbors, so its Hello packets omit them and those neighbors reset the adjacency.
tldr.mechanism: The restarting router sets a new RS (restart signal) bit in the Extended Options TLV of the Link-Local Signaling block in its Hello packets, and neighbors that support it skip the two-way connectivity check while the router resynchronizes.
tldr.outcome: It only works if neighbors support it; those that do not simply reset the adjacency. The RFC records a mechanism that predates Graceful OSPF Restart and is not an IETF standard.

facts.label: Carried in
facts.value: Extended Options TLV of the LLS block

today: RFC 4812 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records a vendor-specific mechanism that came before the standardized Graceful OSPF Restart in RFC 3623.

sections.title: The Restart Problem
sections.content:
During a graceful restart of OSPF software (RFC 3623), a router must stop its neighbors from resetting their adjacencies. After a reload, though, the router may not know which neighbors it had adjacencies with before. If it sends a Hello packet that does not list some neighbors, those neighbors reset the adjacency.

This RFC describes a technique for restarting routers to tell neighbors that they may not know about some neighbors yet, so the absence of some router IDs in the Hello packets should be ignored. The abstract says the mechanism is vendor-specific, was proposed before Graceful OSPF Restart, has at least one major vendor supporting it, and is documented here for public use. It is not an IETF standard.
sections.eli5: When a router wakes up from a reboot it forgets who its friends are. Its friends think it has left and cross it off the list, unless it tells them it is just restarting.

sections.title: The RS Bit
sections.content:
The solution adds a new bit, called RS (restart signal), to the Extended Options (EO) TLV in the Link-Local Signaling (LLS) block defined in RFC 4813. Its value is 0x00000002. It sits next to the LR bit, which is defined in RFC 4811.

A router sets the RS bit in the EO-TLV attached to a Hello packet when it does not know that all neighbors are listed, but wants them to keep their adjacencies. The RS bit must not be set in Hello packets longer than RouterDeadInterval seconds.
sections.eli5: The RS bit is a small flag on the router's greeting that means 'I am restarting, do not forget me.'

sections.title: How Neighbors React
sections.content:
A router that receives a Hello with the RS bit set should skip the two-way connectivity check for that neighbor. That means it should not generate a 1-WayReceived event when it does not find its own router ID in the neighbor list, provided the neighbor state machine for this neighbor is in the Full state. It should also send a unicast Hello back with the RS bit clear, which speeds up learning of previously known neighbors.

Two new fields are added to the neighbor data structure: a RestartState flag and a ResyncTimeout timer. The timer is a single-shot timer lasting RouterDeadInterval seconds. It limits the delay between the first RS-bit Hello and the start of link state database resynchronization using RFC 4811.

  • First RS-bit Hello: set the flag and start the timer.
  • Timer expires: clear the flag and generate a 1-WayReceived event.
  • Neighbor starts resynchronization: cancel the timer, and clear the flag when it completes.
  • Two or more routers on the same segment with RS-bit Hellos at once, as when they restart together: clear the flag, cancel the timer, and generate a 1-WayReceived event.
sections.eli5: The neighbor starts a countdown when it hears 'be right back.' If the router returns and catches up in time, all is fine. If the countdown ends first, the neighbor crosses it off the list.

sections.title: Topology Stability, Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
To avoid possible routing loops, a configurable option on neighbors can make them stop treating the restarting router as fully adjacent. With it, when a router schedules a routing table calculation because its link state database changed, it also resets all adjacencies with restarting routers: it clears their RestartState flags, cancels any running timers, and generates 1-WayReceived events.

The technique needs cooperation from neighbors. If a neighbor does not support it, it will just reset the adjacency. The Security Considerations section says the technique introduces no new security issues into OSPF, and the IANA section points to RFC 4813 for the Extended Options bit definitions.
sections.eli5: If the map changes while the router is away, neighbors stop saving its seat, to be safe. A neighbor that does not know this trick just crosses the router off.
